item.title: Critical phpAfterShell Vulnerability Disclosed in PHP Session Handler
item.description:
Critical phpAfterShell Vulnerability Disclosed in PHP Session Handler

On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a critical vulnerability in PHP’s default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. PHP released official patches to resolve this and 16 other security vulnerabilities on the same day. There is currently no indication that these vulnerabilities have been exploited in the wild.

🔍 Overview

Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, phpAfterShell scores a 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project addressed the flaw in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases also resolve 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of which are similarly rated as critical.

As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities are listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no reviewed sources report active exploitation.

🧩 How it works

PHP stores session data in files by default. The phpAfterShell vulnerability involves the session write and deserialization processes:

  • Session read: When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array.
  • Session write: When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.
  • Interruption: phpAfterShell is triggered when this write operation is interrupted. Following an interruption, the session file can hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the leftover end of the old session data.
  • Deserialization: On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker managed to shape the old session data, PHP can deserialize objects of the attacker’s choosing.

An attacker can shape the stored session data by using PHP’s session upload progress feature (which writes file upload progress into the session) or by targeting applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session. Although PHP notes that code execution requires a write interruption at a useful point and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application, depthfirst reports reaching code execution without any application gadget. They achieved this by chaining phpAfterShell with a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. It is unestablished whether this second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.

⚙️ Mitigation and Protection

To mitigate the vulnerability, Cloudflare has updated its Web Application Firewall (WAF) to block known phpAfterShell attack patterns. These updates build on a PHP remote code execution rule first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities, which has now been updated to cover phpAfterShell.

Rule Name / Feature Target Vulnerability Managed Ruleset Default Action
phpAfterShell Rule CVE-2026-126714 Free and Paid (Enabled by default) Block
PHP-FPM Request Smuggling Rule CVE-2026-129289 Paid Plans (Enabled by default) Log
PHP SOAP Extension Rules CVE-2026-15353, CVE-2026-129506 Paid Plans (Enabled by default) Log

The request smuggling and SOAP rules use the “Log” action by default because the traffic patterns they target can occasionally occur in legitimate traffic. Paid plan customers can review matching requests in Security Events and change the action to “Block” once they verify that legitimate traffic is unaffected.

Cloudflare emphasizes that the WAF serves as an additional layer of defense rather than a complete replacement for patching. Because several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or bypass pathways visible to the WAF, the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart all worker processes.

#PHP #phpAfterShell #Cybersecurity #Cloudflare #Vulnerability

Source: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws

item.title: Critical PHP and Drupal Security Updates Released
item.description:
Critical PHP and Drupal Security Updates Released

On November 19, security updates were released for 18 vulnerabilities in the PHP development ecosystem, alongside the patching of a critical remote code execution flaw in the Drupal content management system. These updates address severe security issues that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable servers.

🚀 PHP Security Updates

The PHP dev team released updates for all supported branches, with versions 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 now available. Security firm Aikido reports that these updates address 18 CVEs affecting PHP’s core engine, session handling, PHP-FPM, CGI, and other components. The most serious flaw, CVE-2026-129289, is a critical PHP-FPM request smuggling vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.2. This vulnerability affects certain nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM; standard configurations that do not reuse connections are not affected. As a temporary mitigation, administrators can disable persistent backend connections to ensure they are closed after each request. Third-party maintainer Ondrej Surý has released patched packages for unsupported versions back to PHP 5.6, and Aikido has released hardened container images for similar unsupported versions.

🧩 PHP Vulnerability Details

The following vulnerabilities were fixed in the November updates:

CVE Identifier Description
CVE-2026-129474 Use-after-free vulnerability involving magic method backtraces
CVE-2026-129496 Timezone cache use-after-free vulnerability
CVE-2026-126714 Vulnerability involving partially overwritten session files
CVE-2026-115560 Session serializer mismatch vulnerability
CVE-2026-129291 PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free vulnerability
CVE-2026-128090 PHAR OpenSSL signature bypass vulnerability

Additional fixes address memory corruption, information disclosure, cross-site scripting, denial-of-service issues, and unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs. As a temporary mitigation for CVE-2026-115560, PHP recommended disabling session upload progress by setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0. This vulnerability was disclosed in an October 23 informational advisory.

🛡️ Drupal Critical Flaws

The Drupal Security Team has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165. Discovered by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, this flaw allows anonymous users to exploit the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, potentially leading to site takeover or remote code execution. The security team warned that at least one critical vulnerability can be exploited by anonymous users. Drupal administrators are urged to upgrade to versions 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13. For those who cannot immediately upgrade, it is recommended to secure the Drupal installer by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file. This update also addresses a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166). The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged five Drupal vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021.

#PHP #Drupal #SecurityUpdates #Vulnerabilities #CVE

item.title: esptool-js brings browser-based serial flashing to Espressif chips
item.description:
esptool-js brings browser-based serial flashing to Espressif chips

esptool-js is a new Javascript implementation of esptool, a serial flasher utility for Espressif chips, that runs directly in supported web browsers using the Web Serial API.

🔍 Overview

The repository provides a tool for flashing firmware to ESP devices without requiring a local Python environment. It is designed to work with Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge version 89 or later, as well as Google Chrome on Android version 61 or later via the web-serial-polyfill compatibility layer.

🧩 How it works

The library operates through the following workflow:

  • Request access to a serial port using the Web Serial API, optionally filtering by USB vendor or product IDs.
  • Configure loader options and create an ESPLoader instance.
  • Connect to the ESP device and detect the chip, a process that resets the device.
  • Flash firmware images to the device.

Users can read firmware files from a File input or fetch request. Key configuration parameters include the starting address in flash, flash mode (e.g., “dio”), flash frequency (e.g., “40m”), and flash size (e.g., “4MB”). Users can also set options to erase the entire flash before writing, compress data during transfer, or reset the device after flashing.

⚙️ Key details

Unlike the Python-based esptool, esptool-js does not implement generation of binary images out of ELF files and does not include companion tools similar to espefuse.py and espsecure.py.

Handling Flash Images

  • Merged .bin files: These are contiguous images where bytes between partitions are 0xFF. Using writeFlash erases every sector from the start of the image through its end, which also erases NVS and factory partitions within that span.
  • Sparse Intel HEX files: These leave gaps out. The parseIntelHex function splits the file into one { data, address } entry per contiguous region. If two regions share a 4 KiB flash sector, parseIntelHex throws an error. To ensure only covered sectors are erased, users should keep eraseAll: false and compress: true.

🚀 Availability

Developers can integrate esptool-js into web applications using the following endpoints:

  • Use https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/bundle.js for a single-file browser load. Dependencies such as pako are inlined, so no import map is required.
  • Use https://unpkg.com/esptool-js/lib/index.js for Node and bundlers. An API documentation reference is available for detailed class and method information.

#Espressif #WebAssembly #JavaScript #IoT #EmbeddedSystems

Source: espressif/esptool-js

item.title: Puppeteer updates installation workflow and adds WebMCP and MCP support
item.description:
Puppeteer updates installation workflow and adds WebMCP and MCP support

Puppeteer, a JavaScript library for controlling Chrome or Firefox, has updated its installation behavior to accommodate modern package manager security defaults, while expanding its capabilities with new API support and an MCP server integration.

🔍 Overview

Puppeteer provides a high-level API to control Chrome or Firefox over the DevTools Protocol or WebDriver BiDi. By default, the tool runs in headless mode, meaning no visible user interface is displayed. Recent developments include the introduction of a Puppeteer-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for browser automation and debugging, as well as support for the experimental WebMCP API.

⚙️ Key details

Modern package managers, including npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun, and Deno, now block dependency install scripts by default. Because Puppeteer traditionally downloaded a compatible Chrome binary during the npm i puppeteer installation step, this security feature can prevent the browser from downloading, leading to runtime errors.

To address this, developers have two main options:

  • Manually download the required browsers after installation by running the command npx puppeteer browsers install.
  • Configure the package manager to allow the specific install script to run. For example, with npm, developers can add “puppeteer” to the “allowScripts” array in the package.json file.

Alternatively, developers can use npm i puppeteer-core to install Puppeteer as a library without automatically downloading Chrome.

🧩 How it works

A standard workflow involves launching a browser instance, opening a new page, navigating to a URL, and interacting with elements using locators and keyboard actions. The library supports querying elements by CSS selectors or by accessible names, allowing for robust interaction with web content.

💡 Why it matters

The updates ensure Puppeteer remains compatible with the default security settings of contemporary package managers while expanding its utility through the installation of the chrome-devtools-mcp server. This allows for enhanced browser automation and debugging workflows.

item.title: New TypeScript AMQP 0-9-1 Client Supports Browsers and Node.js
item.description:
New TypeScript AMQP 0-9-1 Client Supports Browsers and Node.js

A new TypeScript client for AMQP 0-9-1 has been released, supporting both Node.js and browsers via WebSocket. Developed and supported by CloudAMQP, the library is designed to replace other Node.js AMQP libraries and enables developers to write browser applications that communicate directly with AMQP servers.

🔍 Overview

The library is Promise-based, integrating well with async/await, and works with any AMQP 0-9-1 broker, including RabbitMQ, LavinMQ, and Apache Qpid. It supports self-hosted instances and managed providers such as CloudAMQP or Amazon MQ, as they all use the same protocol. The codebase is transpiled from TypeScript, and running Node with the --enable-source-maps flag ensures proper stack traces.

🧩 How it works

The library offers two levels of abstraction:

  • High-level (AMQPSession): Provides automatic reconnection and consumer recovery. Users utilize queue() and exchange() handles for reconnect-safe operations.
  • Low-level (AMQPClient / AMQPWebSocketClient): Offers direct channel access with methods such as queueDeclare, basicPublish, and basicConsume.

The transport mechanism is determined by the URL scheme: amqp:// or amqps:// utilizes TCP, while ws:// or wss:// uses WebSocket. To establish a session with automatic reconnection and consumer recovery, developers call AMQPSession.connect(url, options).

⚙️ Key details

The library is secure by default; publishes are not fulfilled until data is sent on the wire or, if Publish Confirms are enabled on the channel, until the server acknowledges that the message has been enqueued.

Message Acknowledgement

  • Messages are acknowledged after the callback returns.
  • If the callback throws, the message is negatively acknowledged (nacked) and requeued.
  • Developers can override this behavior by calling msg.ack() or msg.nack() directly.
  • Subscriptions created via queue.subscribe() are automatically re-established after a reconnection.
  • The sub.consumerTag and sub.channel properties reflect the current consumer and are updated upon reconnection.
  • Prefetch parameters in subscribe settings can be used to configure Quality of Service (QoS) on each connection.

Codec Registry Developers can opt into a codec registry to handle serialization and deserialization based on content-type and content-encoding:

  • Built-in parsers support JSON and text; built-in coders support gzip and deflate.
  • Defaults can be set to avoid repeating configurations on every publish.
  • When codecs are configured, msg.body contains the decoded value; otherwise, it is a Uint8Array. The CodecMode generic infers this type at compile time.
  • Specific publishes can override defaults by passing contentType or contentEncoding in the options.
  • Custom codecs can be registered by merging them with the built-ins.
  • Decode failures surface as a plain Error rather than an AMQPError; in subscribe() contexts, these failures nack the message, honoring requeueOnNack.

#AMQP #TypeScript #WebSockets #RabbitMQ #Messaging #CloudAMQP

Source: cloudamqp/amqp-client.js

item.title: Datasette Lite: Browser-Based SQLite Database Explorer
item.description:
Datasette Lite: Browser-Based SQLite Database Explorer

Datasette Lite is a port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. It allows users to browse SQLite databases, JSON files, CSV files, or SQL scripts without needing a full web server.

🔍 Overview

  • Datasette Lite enables browsing of SQLite databases, JSON files, CSV files, or SQL scripts directly in the browser.
  • Users can load specific versions of Datasette from PyPI or specific commits, tags, or branches from the Datasette GitHub repository.
  • Over 100 versions of SQLite are available for use with Datasette.
  • Additional Datasette plugins can be installed from PyPI or URLs to wheel files.

🧩 How it works

  • Datasette Lite uses service workers to intercept HTTP requests and serve them from client-side code.
  • Each tab has a unique session ID to ensure that requests are routed to the correct Datasette instance.
  • A web worker runs a dedicated Datasette instance for each session.

⚙️ Key details

  • Datasette Lite can load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions.
  • Users can install additional plugins using the ?install= parameter.
  • SQLite databases, JSON files, CSV files, or SQL scripts can be loaded using the &url= parameter.
  • Metadata files can be loaded using the &metadata= parameter.
  • Fragment hashes can be used to navigate to specific locations within Datasette.

🚀 Availability

  • Datasette Lite is available at lite.datasette.io.

💡 Why it matters

  • Datasette Lite is a powerful tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions.
  • It simplifies the process of demonstrating and fixing bugs by allowing users to share URLs with specific configurations.
  • Datasette Lite is already being used as part of the Datasette development process.

📊 Example

  • Example URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://simonw.github.io/datasette-maplibre/demo.db&metadata=https://simonw.github.io/datasette-maplibre/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

item.title: Chroma.js Library Provides Comprehensive Color Conversion and Scaling Capabilities
item.description:
Chroma.js Library Provides Comprehensive Color Conversion and Scaling Capabilities

Chroma.js is a small-ish zero-dependency JavaScript library for all kinds of color conversions and color scales. It can be installed via npm with npm install chroma-js and imported using import chroma from "chroma-js";.

🔍 Overview

The library supports various color operations:

  • chroma('#D4F880').darken().hex(); returns #a1c550
  • scale = chroma.scale(['white', 'red']); creates a color scale
  • scale(0.5).hex(); returns #FF7F7F

⚙️ Key Features

Chroma.js offers advanced interpolation methods and customization options:

Feature Description
Lab/Lch Interpolation Provides better color interpolation than RGB
Custom Domains Supports custom data domains for scaling
Quantiles Offers quantile-based color scaling
Color Brewer Integrates Color Brewer palettes
Logarithmic Scales Supports logarithmic color scale domains

Example usage:

2

chroma.scale(['white', 'red']).mode('lab');
chroma.scale(['white', 'red']).domain(myValues, 7, 'quantiles');
chroma.scale(['lightyellow', 'navy']).domain([1, 100000], 7, 'log');

The library is written by Gregor Aisch and released under the BSD license. Documentation is available both as an interactive version at http://gka.github.io/chroma.js/ and as a static version on GitHub.

🚀 Availability

Developers can access Chroma.js through multiple channels:

  • Download chroma.min.js directly from GitHub
  • Use the hosted version on unpkg.com
  • Install via npm for Node.js applications
  • Use with SASS through the chromatic-sass package

💡 Development Details

To contribute to Chroma.js:

  • Clone the repository: git clone git@github.com:gka/chroma.js.git
  • Install dev dependencies and compile CoffeeScript source files: npm run build
  • Run tests: npm test
  • Add tests for new features in the /test folder

Note that versions prior to 0.4 were released under the GPL license.

item.title: Chromatone Offers an Open-Source Digital Garden of Visual Music Theory

Chromatone Offers an Open-Source Digital Garden of Visual Music Theory

Chromatone has been introduced as an independent open-source research project to use colors, shapes, and motion to learn, play, and communicate melody, harmony, and rhythms in live music performance environments. It functions as both a digital garden of visual music theory and a collection of visual music instruments.

🔍 Overview

Chromatone provides scientific research on many aspects of music theory as cards and short overviews focusing on the physics and physiology of vision and hearing, alongside their intersection in visual music research, exploration, practice, and self-expression. The project consists of progressive web-apps designed to be carried in a pocket for everyday music practice, including open-source web-experiments featuring interactive combinations of sounds and colors.

🧩 Key Features

  • Interactive Experiments: Open-source tools for sound analysis and synthesis, allowing users to experiment with various media instruments.
  • Modular Music Theory Data: Neatly stored lists of intervals, chords, scales, and rhythmic patterns from different cultures provided in YAML format.
  • Developer Integration: Everything is available as a treeshakeable NPM package that can be integrated into any JS project on both the server-side (SSR) and the client-side.
  • Educational Utility: The project abstracts low-level details into simple building blocks, making it a functional tool for prototyping and concept verification by audio researchers, educators, and students.

item.title: Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly
item.description:
Datasette Lite runs full Python web app in browser via WebAssembly

Datasette Lite allows the full server-side Datasette Python web application to run directly inside a user’s browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide.

🧩 How it works

When the demo is launched, the browser downloads and executes a full Python interpreter, installs the datasette package and its dependencies, and starts the application in a Web Worker.

  • Datasette pages are displayed in a full-window <iframe> pointing to URLs under /app/<session>/.
  • A service worker (sw.js) intercepts requests (link clicks, form submissions, fetch calls, static assets) and relays them to the Datasette ASGI application running in Pyodide.
  • This architecture supports Datasette’s own JavaScript, plugin assets, POST forms, CSRF protection, sign-in cookies, and file uploads/downloads.
  • Streaming responses, such as server-sent events or CSV exports, are processed as they are produced.
  • If a client disconnects or aborts a fetch, the Datasette application is notified that the client has disconnected.
  • Cookies are stored in a cookie jar inside the Python ASGI bridge, lasting until the tab is closed or reloaded.

⚙️ Key details

  • Browser Requirements: Requires a browser with service worker support. Private browsing modes that disable service workers are not compatible.
  • Web Worker Support: Requires module workers (Chrome 80, Safari 15, Firefox 114 or later).
  • Python Version: Uses Python 3.14 from Pyodide 314.0.8.
  • Error Handling:
    • 503 returned if the tab has already been closed or reloaded.
    • 504 returned if the tab stops answering partway through a request (after four minutes).
    • 500 returned if the Pyodide worker itself fails.
    • 409 returned if a tab was opened before an incompatible update.
  • Session Management: Each tab receives a random session identifier, allowing multiple instances with different data to run simultaneously.
  • Navigation: The page mirrors the iframe’s location into its fragment to ensure the back button works and URLs are bookmarkable.
  • Security: Links to external sites open in a new window with noopener.

🚀 Availability and Versioning

Datasette Lite uses the most recent Datasette release from PyPI by default, including alpha and beta previews.

  • Stable Release: Append ?ref=stable to the URL.
  • Specific Release: Pass a version number as ?ref=.
  • Preview Release: ?ref=pre is equivalent to leaving ?ref out.
  • Source Code: Other ?ref values are treated as branches, tags, or commits in the simonw/datasette GitHub repository.
    • Example: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=main runs the latest development code.
    • Short SHAs made up only of digits are read as version numbers; full 40-character SHAs are required for specific commits.
    • ?ref values that look like version numbers are always installed from PyPI.
  • Plugin Installation: ?install= works for plugins, requiring a commit with a pyproject.toml.
  • CORS Handling: GitHub source zip files are downloaded through a Cloudflare Worker to add necessary CORS headers.

#Datasette #WebAssembly #Pyodide #SQLite #Python

Source: simonw/datasette-lite

item.title: Browser Use releases Pi Mono-based web agent with cloud browser support
item.description:
Browser Use releases Pi Mono-based web agent with cloud browser support

Browser Use has announced a new AI web agent built on Pi Mono, described as a tiny TypeScript web agent that hill climbed on real browser evaluations. The agent writes JavaScript, controls Chrome, and builds the helpers it needs dynamically. It uses Pi Mono plus a persistent V8 REPL and raw CDP to enable programmability with sessions, saved logins, streaming and typed results. The implementation is provided as a single SDK that can be integrated into applications via npm install @browser_use/pi, pnpm add @browser_use/pi, or bun add @browser_use/pi. Developers need Node 22.19+ or Bun 1.3.14+ (with Bun requiring Node for the V8 worker). The system uses Browser Use Cloud, so no local Chrome installation is needed, and supports upstream Pi’s model catalog and transports with custom providers, sessions with follow-ups and saved logins, persistent workspaces, and cloud browsers or user-owned Chrome. An ultrafast mode minimizes waits after actions, and the platform provides interaction highlights, recordings, and GIF exports. JavaScript runs in a separate worker with filesystem and network access, while anonymous run counters are enabled by default but can be disabled through telemetry settings or the DO_NOT_TRACK environment variable.

item.title: Managing AI-Generated Pull Request Descriptions with HTML Details and Summary Tags
item.description:
Managing AI-Generated Pull Request Descriptions with HTML Details and Summary Tags

Developers are increasingly utilizing coding agents like Claude Code and Codex to open pull requests (PRs) and manage project changes. While these agents generate accurate and comprehensive descriptions—detailing the problem, the solution, and verification steps—the volume of text can be overwhelming, leading to the use of specific Markdown techniques to organize information for human reviewers.

🧩 How it works

GitHub Markdown supports the HTML <details><summary> elements, which render as a collapsed heading that can be expanded to view larger blocks of text. This feature allows developers to bundle agent-written content behind a concise, human-curated summary:

  • The <summary> tag serves as the clickable line of text that acts as a summary.
  • The <details> element wraps the rest of the content to keep it hidden until expanded.
  • A carefully selected opening paragraph provides a high-level explanation to get readers up to speed.
  • The full agent-written description is placed within the tags to prevent the reader’s eyes from glazing over.
  • Screenshots are sometimes included to quickly illustrate new features.

⚙️ Key details

To maintain clarity, the order of the tags can be remembered using the five-syllable mnemonic “details-summary.” Developers use the summary line to identify the source and intensity of the AI work.

Attribute Usage in PR Summary
Model Name Identifies the specific agent used, such as Claude Opus 5.5.
Effort Level Indicates the intensity of the work, such as “Medium”.
Human Judgement Used to select the short opener or extract a summary from the agent’s text.

💡 Why it matters

Using the <details><summary> structure ensures that the PR remains a functional unit of work for bundling commits and documenting decisions without sacrificing readability. It provides a promise to the reader that the visible text represents human judgment on what is worth their time, while keeping the exhaustive agent-generated verification steps and data accessible for those who need it.

item.title: Datasette Stops Serving Rel Next HTTP Headers to Firefox to Prevent Unnecessary Prefetching
item.description:
Datasette Stops Serving Rel Next HTTP Headers to Firefox to Prevent Unnecessary Prefetching

Datasette issue #3046 proposes no longer serving link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages after discovery that Firefox automatically prefetches the next page of table rows.

🔍 Overview

When reviewing the Firefox network panel, requests to a Datasette table page were found to trigger an HTTP prefetch for the next page of rows in that table. This behavior was caused by Datasette pages serving an HTTP link header formatted as: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next"

⚙️ Key Details

  • Firefox has had an open issue regarding this HTTP prefetching behavior for 24 years.
  • An early comment on that 24-year-old issue links to a 2002 blog post written by the Datasette creator complaining about the feature.
  • The author had forgotten about both writing the blog post and the feature itself.

💡 Why It Matters

Automatic prefetching for next-page table rows creates unnecessary overhead:

  • Only a tiny fraction of visitors click the ’next’ link on a page.
  • The browser ends up fetching unnecessary data.
  • The Datasette server is forced to render an entire page that gets thrown away.

item.title: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) Shapes Content for AI Answer Engines
item.description:
Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) Shapes Content for AI Answer Engines

Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is the emerging practice of preparing web content so that AI‑driven answer engines can retrieve, quote, and verify it as a source.

🔍 Overview

  • GEO “covers every measure that makes a website retrievable, quotable and verifiable for AI answer engines such as Google’s AI search, ChatGPT, Perplexity or Gemini”.
  • Modern search experiences often show a summarised AI answer first, with classic results below (e.g., Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode).
  • The main AI answer systems include:
    • Google AI search (AI Overviews, AI Mode)
    • ChatGPT with integrated web search
    • Perplexity
    • Google Gemini
    • Microsoft Copilot (built on Bing)
  • These systems differ in the index they retrieve content from and how clearly they identify their sources.

🧩 How GEO Works

  1. Passage preparation – The answer engine selects individual passages, not whole pages. Each passage must “stand on its own” and make sense without surrounding context.
  2. Retrieval crawler access – The crawlers that feed AI answers are not the classic Googlebot; they index content specifically for generative use.
  3. Entity consistency – Company name, description, and contact details should be identical everywhere so that the model can reliably identify the entity.

⚙️ Key Details

  • SEO, AEO and GEO describe three stages of the same development:
    • SEO aims at a position in the results list.
    • GEO aims at being cited as a source inside an AI‑written answer.
  • GEO can give visibility “in a place where you would otherwise not appear at all”.
  • GEO does not reliably increase traffic; a prominent AI answer can actually reduce clicks to the original site.
  • Promises that GEO will boost traffic are unfounded.
  • AI answer engines follow a similar source‑selection sequence: they retrieve documents, pick individual passages, combine them into an answer, and link some sources. If a site does not appear in the leading results for a sub‑question, it is usually not considered as a source.

📉 Impact on Website Visits

  • Expect fewer visits to your website when your content is used as a quoted passage in a top‑level AI answer.
  • While GEO raises the chance of being named as a source, it does not guarantee additional clicks.

📚 Managing Access and Training

  • Widely used generative crawlers (as of October 2026) include:
    • GPTBot, OAI‑SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google‑Extended.
  • Blocking specific bots produces targeted effects:
Bot Effect of Blocking
GPTBot Prevents content from being used for model training
OAI-SearchBot Prevents content from appearing in ChatGPT search
Google-Extended Excludes content from generative AI features without affecting normal indexing
  • To stop content from being used for training and still appear in AI answers, the two cases must be handled separately.

🛡️ What GEO Does Not Do

  • GEO does not quote whole pages; only self‑contained sections are used.
  • GEO does not guarantee more traffic; a top‑level answer can actually reduce clicks.
  • Selling GEO as a traffic‑generation solution is misleading.

#GEO #AIsearch #SEO #ContentOptimization

Source: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO): How to Get Cited by AI Search

item.title: VibeGame: Exploring Vibe Coding Games with AI-Assisted Development
item.description:
🎮 VibeGame: Exploring Vibe Coding Games

Published September 29, 2025

By Dylan Ebert

🚨 The Problem

People are trying to vibe code games. And it kind of works, at first. However, as the project grows, things begin to fall apart. Why? And what can we do about it?

I’ll talk about the problem, how I fixed it, and where to go from here.

🤔 What Is “Vibe Coding”?

First, what is vibe coding? It’s originally coined by Andrej Karpathy in a viral tweet where it’s defined as where you “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials and forget the code even exists”.

However, since then, it’s used descriptively to mean a lot of different things, anywhere from just “using AI when coding” to “not thinking about the code at all”. In this blog post, I’ll define it as: using AI as a high-level programming language to build something. Like other programming languages, this benefits from understanding what’s going on under the hood, but doesn’t necessarily require it.

With this interpretation, you could make a game without understanding code, though knowing the fundamentals still helps.

🧠 Context Management

Earlier I mentioned that “as the project grows, things begin to fall apart”. This is because there is evidence that as the context window fills up, model performance begins to degrade. This is especially true for game development, where the context can grow very large, very quickly.

To address this issue, there are many personal ad-hoc solutions, such as writing LLM-specific context directly in the project files, or more comprehensive solutions like Claude Code Development Kit for large-scale context management.

I couldn’t find a lightweight, accessible solution, which doesn’t rely on significant domain knowledge. So I made one: 🧅 Shallot, a simple, lightweight, unopinionated context management system for Claude Code. It relies on two basic commands:

  1. /peel [prompt] to load context at the beginning of a conversation
  2. /nourish to update context at the end of a conversation

Anecdotally, this works well. However, it works best when the project stays lean and well-organized, so all relevant context can easily fit in the model’s context window. While Claude Code is used here, the same principles generalize to other models.

Beyond context management tools, platform choice is critical. The platform should ideally naturally keep projects lean through high-level abstractions, while also being something AI models understand well. So, what existing platforms are best suited for vibe coding?

🔍 Initial Exploration

I initially tried 3 different approaches to vibe coding games: Roblox MCP, Unity MCP, and web. For each, I tried to build a simple incremental game inspired by Grass Cutting Incremental, using Claude Code for each.

Here’s how it went:

⚡ Attempt 1: Roblox MCP

The official MCP server from Roblox. This allows AI to interact with Roblox Studio by sending commands to run code.

Pros:

  • Excellent level of abstraction with built-in game mechanics
  • AI could very easily understand the syntax and convert instructions to code

Cons:

  • No files, only using code to read data, which severely limits context management
  • Very limited runtime information for AI to work with
  • Proprietary walled garden

Roblox provides an excellent layer of abstraction for keeping the codebase lean and manageable, which is perfect for vibe coding. However, the walled garden and lack of context makes it infeasible for vibe coding, unless it’s in-house at Roblox.

🎯 Attempt 2: Unity MCP

The unofficial MCP server for Unity. This allows AI to interact with the Unity Editor: reading the console, managing assets, and validating scripts.

Pros:

  • Full file system access

Cons:

  • There are many ways to do everything in Unity, changing frequently across versions, causing AI to get confused
  • Requires significant domain knowledge to tell the AI how to do things, rather than what to do
  • AI performance was inconsistent and unreliable
  • Proprietary engine (though much more transparent than Roblox)

Unity is a powerful engine with a lot of capabilities. However, the complexity and variability of the engine makes it difficult for AI to consistently produce good results without significant user domain knowledge.

🌐 Attempt 3: Web Stack

The open web platform, using three.js for 3D rendering, rapier for physics, and bitecs for game logic.

Pros:

  • Far superior AI proficiency compared to game engines, likely due to massive training data
  • Full file system access
  • Fully open source stack with complete control/transparency

Cons:

  • Relatively low level libraries, requiring essentially building the engine before building the game
  • Lack of ecosystem for high-quality 3D games; web tends toward 2D games and simple 3D experiences

This approach had the best AI performance by far, likely due to the vast amount of web development data available during training. However, the low-level nature of the libraries meant that I had to essentially build a game engine before I could build the game itself. This allows us to work at a much higher level of abstraction, like we did with Roblox.

Although it required building an engine first, this approach was the only one that produced a fun result without heavy domain knowledge.

📊 Comparison Summary

Platform AI Performance Abstraction Level Context Management Open Source
Roblox ⭐⭐⭐ ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ⭐ ❌
Unity ⭐ ⭐⭐ ⭐⭐⭐ ❌
Web ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ⭐ ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ✅

🚀 The Solution: VibeGame

After these experiments, I had a clear picture: the web stack had excellent AI performance but was too low-level, while Roblox had perfect abstraction but lacked openness and context management.

So, what about combining the best of both?

Introducing VibeGame, a high-level declarative game engine built on top of three.js, rapier, and bitecs, designed specifically for AI-assisted game development.

🎨 Design Philosophy

There were three key decisions that went into the design of VibeGame:

  1. Abstraction: A high-level abstraction with built-in features like physics, rendering, and common game mechanics, keeping the codebase lean and manageable. This takes inspiration from popular high-level sandbox games/game “engines” like Roblox, Fortnite UEFN, and Minecraft.

  2. Syntax: A declarative XML-like syntax for defining game objects and their properties, making it easy for AI to understand and generate code. This is similar to HTML/CSS, which AI models are already proficient in.

  3. Architecture: An Entity-Component-System (ECS) architecture for scalability and flexibility. ECS separates data (components) from behavior (systems), encouraging the project to stay modular and organized as it grows, conducive to vibe coding and context management.

A basic game looks like this:

 1
 2
 3
 4
 5
 6

10
11

13
14

<world canvas="#game-canvas" sky="#87ceeb">
 <!-- Ground -->
 <static-part pos="0 -0.5 0" shape="box" size="20 1 20" color="#90ee90"></static-part>

 <!-- Ball -->
 <dynamic-part pos="-2 4 -3" shape="sphere" size="1" color="#ff4500"></dynamic-part>
</world>

<canvas id="game-canvas"></canvas>

<script type="module">
 import * as GAME from 'vibegame';
 GAME.run();
</script>

See it in action in this JSFiddle or the Live Demo.

This will create a simple scene with a ground plane and a falling ball. The player, camera, and lighting are created automatically. All of this is modular and can be replaced. Arbitrary custom components and systems can be added as needed.

This comes bundled with an llms.txt file containing documentation about the engine, designed specifically for AI, to be included in its system prompt or initial context.

✅ So Does It Actually Work?

Yes.

Well, kind of.

Here’s the game I built to test building a simple incremental grass collection game using VibeGame and Claude Code. It worked very well, requiring minimal domain knowledge for implementing the core game mechanics.

![Grass Cutting Game](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/m ain/blog/vibegame/grass_cutting_game.gif)

Simple grass cutting incremental game built with VibeGame

However, there are still some major caveats:

  1. It works well for building what the game engine supports, i.e. a simple platformer or game that only relies on basic physics and rendering.
  2. However, it struggles with anything more complex that isn’t yet implemented in the engine, like interaction, inventory, multiplayer, combat, etc.

So, with a definition of vibe coding that is the one-shot “make me a game” approach, it doesn’t work. However, with the definition of treating vibe coding like a high-level programming language, it works very well, but requires users to understand the engine’s capabilities and limitations.

🛠️ Try It Yoursel

To try it immediately, I built a demo where you can develop a game directly in the browser using VibeGame with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct: Live Demo on Hugging Face.

You can also test it locally with a frontier model like Claude Code:

1
2
3

npm create vibegame@latest my-game
cd my-game
npm run dev # or bun dev

Then, paste all the contents of the included llms.txt to CLAUDE.md, providing full documentation about the engine for the AI to reference (or point your own context management system to it). This works with other models as well.

🔮 What’s Next?

The engine is currently very barebones and only supports very basic mechanics (unless writing it from scratch). However, initial results are promising.

Next steps would be:

  1. Flesh out the engine with more built-in mechanics, getting closer to par with early versions of Roblox or UEFN. This includes:

    • Interaction
    • Inventory/items
    • Multiplayer
    • Skinned meshes/animations with curated database
    • Audio with curated database

  2. Improve the AI guidance systems, providing beginners with a better experience. This includes:

    • Clear messaging about engine capabilities/limitations
    • Guided prompts for common tasks
    • Many more examples and templates
    • Educational resources

It’s also worth exploring how vibe coding games could harness more proven engines. For example, building a high-level sandbox game editor on top of Unity or Unreal Engine (similar to how Unreal Editor for Fortnite is built on Unreal Engine) could provide a more controlled environment for AI to work with, while leveraging the power of established engines.

We’re also likely to see more in-house solutions from major players.

Follow me to keep up with what’s going on in the space!

🔗 Links:

  • VibeGame
  • Hugging Face Demo
  • Example Game (made with VibeGame)
  • Shallot Context Manager

🙌 Credits

Originally posted at: https://huggingface.co/blog/vibegame

🏁 Conclusion

VibeGame represents an innovative approach to bridging the gap between AI capabilities and game development accessibility. While current limitations prevent true one-shot game creation, the engine successfully demonstrates how high-level abstractions combined with AI-friendly syntax can enable rapid prototyping and development of simple games.

The key insight is that vibe coding works best when treated as a high-level programming language rather than magic. By providing the right tools, abstractions, and context management systems, we can harness AI’s strengths while working within its current limitations.

As AI models continue to improve and game engines become more AI-friendly, we’re likely to see even more sophisticated solutions emerge from both indie developers and major industry players.

🔮 Beyond Expectations: Running Real-Time Conversational AI Locally with GLTF Avatar Animation

Summary: Discover how local conversational AI models are exceeding performance expectations and explore the exciting frontier of integrating these models with 3D avatar animations through ThreeJS and GLTF in browsers.

🚀 The Surprising Power of Local AI Implementations

When it comes to conversational AI, we’ve grown accustomed to cloud-dependent solutions that require constant internet connectivity and raise privacy concerns. But what if I told you that running these sophisticated models 100% locally is not only possible—it’s impressively effective?

“𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘣𝘦𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘯 𝘐 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥!” This revelation isn’t just exciting—it’s transformative for how we conceptualize AI integration in everyday applications.

Local AI processing is experiencing a renaissance moment. Modern devices pack enough computational power to handle increasingly optimized models without sacrificing performance. The advantages are compelling:

  • 🔒 Enhanced privacy with data never leaving your device
  • ⚡ Zero latency from network communication
  • 🌐 Offline functionality in any environment
  • 💰 Reduced operational costs without cloud processing fees

The initial success of these local implementations naturally leads to the question: what’s next? The answer appears to be bringing these conversational models to life through visual representation.

🤖 The Next Frontier: Animated AI Avatars

The logical progression from effective local conversational AI is visual embodiment. As noted in the original observation: “𝙎𝙤 𝙩𝙝𝙚𝙣 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙣𝙚𝙭𝙩 𝙤𝙗𝙫𝙞𝙤𝙪𝙨 𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙥 𝙞𝙨 𝙖𝙫𝙖𝙩𝙖𝙧 𝙖𝙣𝙞𝙢𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣…𝙨𝙤𝙢𝙚𝙝𝙤𝙬.”

This integration introduces fascinating technical challenges and opportunities. For browser-based applications, the technology stack seems clearly defined:

  • 📦 GLTF (GL Transmission Format) avatars as the 3D model standard
  • 🎭 ThreeJS as the rendering engine
  • 🗣️ Phoneme animation to synchronize speech with facial movements

GLTF has emerged as the “JPEG of 3D” for good reason. The format efficiently packages textures, materials, and animations in a web-friendly way, making it ideal for browser-based AI avatars.

🧩 Building the Technical Stack for Animated AI Companions

Let’s explore what this integration might look like from a technical perspective.

The Foundation: Local Conversational AI

At the core is a lightweight, optimized language model capable of running entirely on-device. Recent innovations in model quantization, pruning, and architecture optimization have made this possible even on modest hardware. These models can process natural language, generate contextually appropriate responses, and maintain conversation state without external dependencies.

function handleUserInput(text) {
 const response = await conversation.getResponse(text);
 generateSpeech(response);
 animateAvatar(response);
}

The Visual Layer: ThreeJS and GLTF

ThreeJS provides the perfect foundation for rendering 3D content in browsers with WebGL. Combined with GLTF models, you can create expressive avatars that run smoothly across devices:

const loader = new GLTFLoader();

loader.load('avatar.gltf', (gltf) => {
 const avatar = gltf.scene;
 scene.add(avatar);

 // Extract animation mixers and facial morphs
 const mixer = new THREE.AnimationMixer(avatar);
 const morphTargetDictionary = avatar.morphTargetDictionary;
});

The Animation Challenge: Phoneme Mapping

The most technically complex piece is synchronizing speech with facial movements through phoneme animation. Phonemes—the distinct units of sound in language—need to be mapped to facial expressions:

 phonemes.forEach(({phoneme, startTime, duration}) => {
 setTimeout(() => {
 const morphIndex = morphTargetDictionary[phonemeToMorphMap[phoneme]];
 avatar.morphTargetInfluences[morphIndex] = 1.0;

 // Blend to next phoneme
 setTimeout(() => {
 avatar.morphTargetInfluences[morphIndex] = 0.0;
 }, duration);
 }, startTime);
 });
}

🔍 Real-World Applications and Future Potential

This technology combination opens doors to numerous applications:

  • 🎓 Educational assistants with engaging visual presence
  • 🏥 Healthcare companions for patient interaction
  • 🛒 Retail customer service with personalized avatars
  • 🎮 Gaming NPCs with dynamic conversational abilities
  • 🌐 Accessible web interfaces for diverse user needs

The most exciting aspect is how this technology democratizes access to embodied AI. Rather than requiring specialized hardware or expensive cloud services, these solutions can run on common devices already in users’ hands.

🌟 Looking Forward: The Human Touch

As we develop these avatar-enhanced conversational systems, the key challenge will be balancing technical capability with human-like interaction. The uncanny valley—that unsettling feeling when something appears almost but not quite human—remains a significant hurdle.

The path forward likely involves:

  1. 🎨 Stylized rather than photorealistic avatars
  2. 🎭 Expressive but not exaggerated animations
  3. 🧠 Context-aware emotional responses
  4. 🔄 Natural conversation flow with appropriate pauses and reactions

What’s particularly exciting about this development is how it bridges the gap between pure text interaction and fully embodied AI. The combination of local processing power with visual representation creates a more engaging, accessible AI experience.

As these technologies continue to mature, we might soon find ourselves having meaningful conversations with AI companions that not only understand what we’re saying but respond with appropriate facial expressions and gestures—all running entirely on our personal devices.

The question now becomes: how will these visual representations shape our relationships with AI systems? Will animated avatars create stronger emotional connections to artificial intelligence, and how might that transform our digital interactions?

🚀 Holo1-3B: The Open-Source VLM Redefining Web Automation Cost-Efficiency

𝙎𝙪𝙢𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙮: HCompany’s new Holo1-3B model delivers state-of-the-art web automation capabilities at a fraction of the cost of GPT-4 alternatives. This Action Vision-Language Model powers the Surfer-H web agent system with impressive accuracy on UI localization tasks while offering the best accuracy-to-cost ratio in the industry.

🔍 Introduction: Web Agents That See and Act Like Humans

In today’s rapidly evolving AI landscape, the ability for models to interact with web interfaces like humans do represents a significant frontier. Web automation traditionally required complex programming, brittle selectors, or expensive API solutions. But what if an AI could simply look at a website and identify where to click, just as a human would?

That’s exactly what HCompany has achieved with their new Holo1-3B model, an open-source Vision-Language Model (VLM) specifically built for web automation. Designed as part of the Surfer-H web agent system, it demonstrates remarkable capabilities that position it as a compelling alternative to expensive proprietary solutions.

Let’s explore why this matters and how this technology could transform how we automate web interactions.

🧠 Understanding Holo1 and Surfer-H Architecture

Holo1 isn’t just another VLM—it’s an Action Vision-Language Model specifically optimized for web interaction. As part of the Surfer-H agent architecture, it acts in one of three critical roles:

  • 𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: Makes decisions and plans the agent’s behavior
  • 𝗟𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: Visually understands UI elements to enable precise interactions
  • 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: Verifies whether actions produced the desired results

What sets Surfer-H apart is its human-like approach to web navigation—it thinks before acting, takes notes, and can retry if its answer is rejected. Rather than relying on custom APIs or brittle DOM selectors, it operates purely through the browser interface, just as a human would.

The system’s modular design allows for flexible configuration with different models for each component, enabling strategic tradeoffs between accuracy, speed, and cost.

💰 Pareto-Optimal Performance: Better Results at Lower Costs

When evaluated on the WebVoyager benchmark—a collection of 643 real-world web tasks ranging from price checking to event scheduling—Holo1-powered agents delivered remarkable results:

  • 🔥 Surfer-H + Holo1-7B: 92.2% accuracy at $0.13 per task
  • 🔥 Surfer-H + Holo1-3B: 89.7% accuracy at $0.11 per task

For comparison, proprietary alternatives achieved:

  • GPT-4.1: 92.0% accuracy at $0.54 per task
  • GPT-4.1-mini: 88.8% accuracy at $0.26 per task

This positions Holo1 on the Pareto frontier—delivering the best accuracy per dollar spent. At approximately 1/5th the cost of GPT-4.1 for similar performance, the economic implications for organizations deploying web automation at scale are substantial.

🎯 Excelling at UI Localization

A critical skill for web agents is UI localization—identifying precisely where to click or interact with a user interface. Holo1 demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks:

  • Screenspot
  • Screenspot-V2
  • Screenspot-Pro
  • GroundUI-Web
  • WebClick (HCompany’s new benchmark)

This localization capability is what enables Holo1 to interact with websites like a human would—by visually identifying UI elements rather than relying on hidden code structures that might change frequently.

🛠️ Getting Started with Holo1-3B

The best part? Holo1-3B is available now and relatively simple to implement. Based on the Qwen2.5-VL architecture, it’s accessible through Hugging Face’s transformers library.

Here’s a simplified implementation workflow:

  1. Load the model and processor:

2
3

 "Hcompany/Holo1-3B",
 torch_dtype="auto",
 device_map="auto",
)

  1. Process images with care: Since Holo1 uses absolute pixel coordinates, make sure to use the provided smart_resize function to ensure coordinate accuracy.

  2. Choose your interaction style:

    • Simple click coordinates: x, y
    • Structured JSON output for more complex interactions
    • Full navigation steps with rich context awareness

instruction = "Select July 14th as the check-out date"
prompt = localization.get_localization_prompt(image, instruction)
coordinates = run_inference(prompt)[0]

task = "Book a hotel in Paris on August 3rd for 3 nights"
prompt = navigation.get_navigation_prompt(task, image, step=1)
navigation_str = run_inference(prompt)[0]

🔮 The Future of Web Automation

Holo1-3B represents a significant step toward accessible, cost-effective web automation that works like a human user would. Its open-source nature and impressive performance metrics position it as a viable alternative to much more expensive proprietary solutions.

The implications extend beyond simple cost savings. By making sophisticated web automation more accessible, Holo1 could democratize automation capabilities that were previously available only to organizations with significant AI budgets.

As models like Holo1 continue to evolve, we might see entirely new categories of applications emerge—from personalized web assistants to enterprise-scale automation solutions that operate through visual interfaces rather than APIs or code.

🤔 Final Thoughts

When we consider the trajectory of AI development, models like Holo1-3B reveal an important shift: from general-purpose models to specialized systems that excel at specific, high-value tasks. This specialization enables better performance at lower costs, making capabilities more accessible to a wider range of users and organizations.

As we move forward, will we see more domain-specialized models outperform general-purpose alternatives? And how might this change the economics of AI deployment across industries?
